ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Data collection was approved by the University of Washington IRB (#00006464, "Project SMS").
All study procedures were online and approved by the local institutional review board.

Method: Participants were young adults at baseline (n = 496, aged 18-22, Mage = 20.3, SD = 1.3) recruited from the Pacific Northwest who reported drinking or using cannabis "about once per week" or more over the past three months.
Participants completed a baseline assessment and about 32 days of ecological momentary assessments, answering questions about negative emotionality, social withdrawal, urgency, and their alcohol use.
Participants were recruited as part of a larger project on the development of alcohol and cannabis use during adolescence and young adulthood (R01 DA047247).
Participants were young adults at baseline (n = 496, aged 18-22, Mage = 20.3, SD = 1.3).

Participants were recruited from King, Pierce, and Snohomish Counties in Washington State from both college and noncollege sources via internet advertisements on social media and non-internet methods like newspaper advertisements and flyers.

Participants were required to be between the ages of 18 and 22 at study screening, own a smartphone, be fluent in English, and reported drinking or using cannabis "about once per week" or more over the past 3 months.
Participants were excluded if they were not fluent in English or if they moved to the United States after age 12.
Eligible participants completed an online survey and a virtual training session on the study procedures with research assistants.
Following onboarding, participants were texted links to 5 surveys a day, from Thursday-Sunday, with only a single survey on Monday for 8 weeks (i.e., about 32 days of EMA).
Finally, participants completed up to four 45-minute follow-up surveys over the span of 2 years, with one survey every six months starting from their onboarding date.

Participants were compensated up to $451 for completing all study tasks. $50 for the onboarding meeting and baseline survey, $40 for the 6-and 12-month follow-up surveys, $50 for the 18-and 24-month follow-up surveys, and $1 per EMA survey (up to $176) with a $5 bonus for completing at least 80% of the EMAs each week (up to $40).
Some participants were compensated $5 for providing feedback on the protocol.
Each morning from Thursday to Monday, participants were also asked about drinking that occurred the previous day (or during the second assessment of the day if they missed the morning assessment).

Participants were asked to rate how much each statement represents them (e.g., "I often make matters worse because I act without thinking when I am upset) on a 1-4 Likert scale where1 = agree strongly and4 = disagree strongly, meaning that lower scores represent higher endorsement (α=, Ω= ).
Participants are asked to rank their responses to the following prompt, "How often have you experienced the following in the past 12 months," on a 5-point Likert scale.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

Participants completed a baseline assessment and about 32 days of ecological momentary assessments, answering questions about negative emotionality, social withdrawal, urgency, and their alcohol use.
Participants were recruited as part of a larger project on the development of alcohol and cannabis use during adolescence and young adulthood (R01 DA047247).
Participants were young adults at baseline (n = 496, aged 18-22, Mage = 20.3, SD = 1.3).

Participants were recruited from King, Pierce, and Snohomish Counties in Washington State from both college and noncollege sources via internet advertisements on social media and non-internet methods like newspaper advertisements and flyers.

Participants were required to be between the ages of 18 and 22 at study screening, own a smartphone, be fluent in English, and reported drinking or using cannabis "about once per week" or more over the past 3 months.
Participants were excluded if they were not fluent in English or if they moved to the United States after age 12.
Eligible participants completed an online survey and a virtual training session on the study procedures with research assistants.
Following onboarding, participants were texted links to 5 surveys a day, from Thursday-Sunday, with only a single survey on Monday for 8 weeks (i.e., about 32 days of EMA).
Finally, participants completed up to four 45-minute follow-up surveys over the span of 2 years, with one survey every six months starting from their onboarding date.

Participants were compensated up to $451 for completing all study tasks. $50 for the onboarding meeting and baseline survey, $40 for the 6-and 12-month follow-up surveys, $50 for the 18-and 24-month follow-up surveys, and $1 per EMA survey (up to $176) with a $5 bonus for completing at least 80% of the EMAs each week (up to $40).
Some participants were compensated $5 for providing feedback on the protocol.
Each morning from Thursday to Monday, participants were also asked about drinking that occurred the previous day (or during the second assessment of the day if they missed the morning assessment).

Participants were asked to rate how much each statement represents them (e.g., "I often make matters worse because I act without thinking when I am upset) on a 1-4 Likert scale where1 = agree strongly and4 = disagree strongly, meaning that lower scores represent higher endorsement (α=, Ω= ).
Participants are asked to rank their responses to the following prompt, "How often have you experienced the following in the past 12 months," on a 5-point Likert scale.

It is reasonable to assume that COVID-19 lockdowns may have encouraged more solitary drinking or drinking that occurred while participants were physically alone but virtually present with others (e.g., Zoom drinking).
Participants were asked whether their school or work was currently closed due to COVID-19.

Since participants were all from the King, Pierce, and Snohomish counties in Washington state, we can also use the date their data were recorded and cross-reference it with the stage of restrictions publicly announced at the time.

info.title: Testing the solitary drinking component of the social-contextual framework for AUD risk among young adults using Directed Acyclic Graphs

text.text: Objective: Solitary drinking is a low base rate behavior present in some young adults that could be an indicator for the development of later alcohol use problems.

The present work will use a combination of observational data, Directed Acyclic Graphs, and latent variable models to test a between-person causal model of the role of solitary drinking in the etiology of alcohol use disorder risk in young adults.

Method: Participants were young adults at baseline (n = 496, aged 18-22, Mage = 20.3, SD = 1.3) recruited from the Pacific Northwest who reported drinking or using cannabis "about once per week" or more over the past three months.
Participants completed a baseline assessment and about 32 days of ecological momentary assessments, answering questions about negative emotionality, social withdrawal, urgency, and their alcohol use.
Results: will be added at Stage 2.
Significance statement: will be added at Stage 2.
Seventy-five percent of adolescents and young adults aged 18-25 in the United States have consumed alcohol (Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration [SAMHSA], 2023).
However most young adults do not develop drinking problems.
For instance, in 2023 about 15% of young adults met criteria for an alcohol use disorder (AUD; SAMHSA, 2023).
Given most young adults drink, but only some develop drinking problems, it is important to understand how and why some people develop an AUD, while others do not.

Although social influences on drinking have long been a focus of study (Chassin et al., 2016; Sher et al., 2005), more recent research has suggested that the social context of drinking episodes themselves may be a distinct risk factor (Corbin et al., 2020; Creswell, 2021; Creswell et al., 2014 Creswell et al., , 2022;; S. E. King et al., 2025; Skrzynski & Creswell, 2020; Waddell & Acuff, 2025).

text.text: Directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) are an accessible approach to causal inference due to their graphical nature.
They force researchers to make their causal assumptions explicit, often revealing assumptions we may not be aware of otherwise.
Finally, they provide us with a logical way to decide which variables to include as covariates in our statistical models (Deffner et al., 2022; McElreath, 2020; Rohrer, 2018 Rohrer, , 2024)).

text.text: In the present study, we used DAGs to illustrate more clearly what we mean by a "confound" and provide a framework to guide our decisions about which confounds we should and should not statistically adjust for in our models if we wish to observe causal effects.
It is important to note that simply creating a DAG with ones' causal assumptions does not mean that the DAG is correct.
Instead, most DAGs are wrong or incomplete.
They may be missing variables, have arrows misplaced, or contain unobserved confounds that we failed to consider.

text.text: Figure 1 displays one of our DAGs.
We explain how we developed this DAG as a quick tutorial for unfamiliar readers.

We started with existing data where trait constructs from solitary drinking theory (i.e., anxiety/depression, social withdrawal, drinking motives) and negative urgency are measured at baseline and drinking episodes are measured subsequently via daily EMA.
Since trait measures occurred before we observed drinking episodes, we assume trait scores have some causal effect on drinking episodes due to temporal sequencing (Reichenbach, 1991).
text.formatted: Since trait measures occurred before we observed drinking episodes, we assume trait scores have some causal effect on drinking episodes due to temporal sequencing <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Reichenbach, 1991)</ref>.

text.text: So, there are arrows from all four baseline measures into solitary drinking.

We included negative urgency, the tendency to respond impulsively to negative affect (Cyders & Smith, 2007; Whiteside & Lynam, 2009), even though it was not mentioned in a recent solitary drinking conceptual framework (Creswell, 2021) for two reasons.
text.formatted: We included negative urgency, the tendency to respond impulsively to negative affect <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Cyders & Smith, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Whiteside & Lynam, 2009)</ref>, even though it was not mentioned in a recent solitary drinking conceptual framework <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Creswell, 2021)</ref> for two reasons.

text.text: Firstly, negative urgency could be a common cause of both coping motives and solitary drinking.

For example, if solitary drinking behavior represents a coping response to negative affect (Cooper, 2015, p. 25; Creswell, 2021), individuals high in both negative urgency and coping motives may be at particularly elevated risk.

text.text: Secondly, negative urgency is associated with, and could be a facet of the broader construct of, negative emotionality (K. M. King et al., 2014; Sharma et al., 2014).

text.text: This is why we chose to favor negative urgency over other facets of impulsivity in our DAG.

Since our anxiety/depression measure is a broad indicator of negative emotionality, we assume it has some causal effect on social withdrawal and negative urgency because we think of these constructs as more specific expressions of negative emotionality (i.e., arrows from AnxDep to SocWithdrawal and Urg).

These three traits related to negative emotionality then cause drinking to cope motives because we think people who say they experience more negative emotionality on average (anxiety/depression), who say they tend to isolate from others (social withdrawal), or who say then tend to act impulsively when feeling negatively (negative urgency) will recall more memories of drinking to cope while completing the survey.
So, there are arrows from anxiety/depression, negative urgency, and social withdrawal into coping motives.
Note.

AnxDep = Anxiety/Depression score from Achenbach Adult Self-Report; SocWithdrawal = Social Withdrawal from Achenbach Adult Self-Report; Urg = Negative Urgency from UPPS-P; SolDrinks = The proportion of drinking episodes that were solitary from 32 days of EMA.

We think anxiety/depression, social withdrawal, and negative urgency are common causes of coping motives and solitary drinking, so part of the association between coping motives and solitary drinking is confounded.
By adjusting for anxiety/depression, social withdrawal, and negative urgency in the model, we close these confounding paths between coping motives and solitary drinking.

Assuming this DAG represents the true data generating model in the population, when we include anxiety/depression, social withdrawal, and negative urgency in a regression with drinking to cope motives predicting solitary drinking, we will observe the causal effect of coping motives on solitary drinking.

text.text: Participants were young adults at baseline (n = 496, aged 18-22, Mage = 20.3, SD = 1.3).

Participants were recruited from King, Pierce, and Snohomish Counties in Washington State from both college and noncollege sources via internet advertisements on social media and non-internet methods like newspaper advertisements and flyers.
Recruitment began in August 2020 and was completed in November of 2022.

Participants were required to be between the ages of 18 and 22 at study screening, own a smartphone, be fluent in English, and reported drinking or using cannabis "about once per week" or more over the past 3 months.
Participants were excluded if they were not fluent in English or if they moved to the United States after age 12.
All study procedures were online and approved by the local institutional review board.
Eligible participants completed an online survey and a virtual training session on the study procedures with research assistants.
Following onboarding, participants were texted links to 5 surveys a day, from Thursday-Sunday, with only a single survey on Monday for 8 weeks (i.e., about 32 days of EMA).
Finally, participants completed up to four 45-minute follow-up surveys over the span of 2 years, with one survey every six months starting from their onboarding date.

Participants were compensated up to $451 for completing all study tasks. $50 for the onboarding meeting and baseline survey, $40 for the 6-and 12-month follow-up surveys, $50 for the 18-and 24-month follow-up surveys, and $1 per EMA survey (up to $176) with a $5 bonus for completing at least 80% of the EMAs each week (up to $40).
Some participants were compensated $5 for providing feedback on the protocol.
We define solitary drinking as drinking that occurred while physically alone.
At each EMA, participants reported who they were with during the past hour with a "check-all that apply" question.
Responses included friend(s), romantic partner(s), family member(s), stranger(s), acquaintance(s), friend(s) of a friend, roommate(s), coworker(s), classmate(s), Other, and, no one; I was alone.
Only a response of "no one; I was alone," will be used to indicate solitary drinking context.
Each morning from Thursday to Monday, participants were also asked about drinking that occurred the previous day (or during the second assessment of the day if they missed the morning assessment).
Participants reported whether they drank that day, how many drinks they had, when they started drinking, and for how many hours they drank.
We will use social context data from EMAs that overlap with each drinking episode to characterize whether the drinking episode was social or solitary.
Drinking episodes will be characterized as solitary only if participants reported being alone for all EMAs collected during the drinking episode.

text.text: We will test our hypotheses using a Bayesian latent variable modelling approach which we tested on simulated data and an independent pilot dataset.

In aim 1, our goal is to estimate the causal effects of negative emotionality, social discomfort, negative urgency, and coping motives on solitary drinking among young adults guided by Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs).

To achieve aim 1, we will estimate latent variables for negative emotionality, social discomfort, negative urgency, and coping motives and use these latent scores in a binomial regression within the same model to predict the proportion of solitary drinking episodes we observed during the 32-day EMA period.
In short, we will create Bayesian structural equation models.
Then we will observe how coefficients differ across models to update our beliefs about the true DAG in the population.

For example, if the effect of coping motives on solitary drinking shrinks when we close backdoor paths by adding negative emotionality, social discomfort, and negative urgency as covariates, this would strengthen our confidence that our DAG resembles the true data generating model in the population.
If the association instead grows, this will alert us there may be a confound, collider, or descendant in the true data generating model that our DAG did not account for.
See the R script for all model details.
In aim 2, our primary analytic goal is to estimate the causal effect of solitary drinking on future alcohol use disorder symptoms.
The count of solitary drinking and total drinking episodes will be used as predictors along with latent psychological constructs and other backdoor variables.
Alcohol use disorder symptoms will be the binomial outcome.
The number of trials for our binomial outcome will be 11 since that is the total number of possible AUD criterion in the AUDDCSI, and the number of criterion endorsed will be the number of successes.
We use a binomial model because the AUDDCSI is a count variable, not a continuous variable.
We will update our beliefs about the true DAG in the population by observing how the effect of solitary drinking episodes on alcohol use disorder symptoms changes as we close backdoor paths.
We will be attentive to potential unobserved confounds, colliders, or descendants present in the true data generating model that our DAG did not account for.
See the R script for all model details.
In aim 3, our goal is to estimate how one's level of solitary drinking causes different AUD symptom trajectories.
To achieve this, we will estimate growth curve models testing the effect of solitary drinking on the rate of change of AUD symptoms from baseline over two years with observations every 6-months.
We except the effect of solitary drinking episodes on AUD symptom trajectories to decrease as we close backdoor paths.

If people who solitary drink more develop increasing AUD symptoms over time, we should see a positive effect where greater solitary drinking leads to an escalation of AUD symptoms up to 2 years later, even after closing backdoor paths.
This would strengthen existing evidence supporting solitary drinking as a causal risk factor for future AUD in young adults.
We will consider unobserved confounds, colliders, or descendants that might be present in the true data generating model that our DAG did not account for.
See the R script for all model details.
We took many precautions to avoid convergence errors, but there might be complications we cannot anticipate.
If the Bayesian measurement models fail to converge despite optimization attempts, we will first try the same models in Mplus.
If the Mplus models fail to converge, we will use mean scores for the latent constructs within brms binomial regression models instead.

When estimating latent variables within brms, all items contributing to a factor will be mean centered prior to factor estimation.
